reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it is presented as an informational technology news podcast covering multiple stories. Its tech-support-scam segment reports on criminals using fake Microsoft-like malware pop-ups, a phone number, and a credit-card request, while advising listeners not to fall for the scheme and explaining that the pop-up can be removed by the user.

citations.quote: Welcome to Tech News Today, a podcast about keeping you informed and empowered by giving.
Cybercriminals have been busy lately. One of their latest schemes is circulating another tech support scam.
The sites are built to display a pop-up message that looks like a Microsoft notification saying your computer is infected with malware.
The message contains a phone number that you're supposed to call to get rid of the infection.
If you call the number, you'll be speaking with crooks who ask you for your credit card. To pay for their help getting rid of the malware.

opening.argument: The segment describes a concrete action-and-payment pathway: viewers encountering the purported malware warning are told to call a phone number, and the callers are asked for credit-card payment for assistance. That is a direct solicitation tied to obtaining paid remediation, even if the program characterizes the operators negatively. The unusually simple sequence—call, provide card details, receive help—supports treating the described offer as a scam-like acquisition flow rather than merely abstract cybersecurity commentary.

citations.quote: The message contains a phone number that you're supposed to call to get rid of the infection.
If you call the number, you'll be speaking with crooks who ask you for your credit card.
To pay for their help getting rid of the malware.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the segment a warning does not remove the concrete solicitation it presents. The opening itself confirms the essential mechanics: a phone call is connected to a credit-card payment for malware removal. It assumes the audience will accept the narrator's characterization of the callers without independently establishing that the described flow is only reportage rather than material that could steer viewers toward it.

citations.quote: The message contains a phone number that you're supposed to call to get rid of the infection.
If you call the number, you'll be speaking with crooks who ask you for your credit card.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted action is explicitly attributed to criminals operating the hoax, not requested from this program's audience. The segment tells viewers, "Don't fall for it," and instead explains how to close the pop-up themselves. A described payment demand is not a reward, asset acquisition, or offer made by the video.

citations.quote: The problem is, it's a scam.
Don't fall for it.
Just click on the Windows search box in the lower left corner and search for Task Manager.

opening.argument: Several classic deception signals appear together in the described flow: malicious advertisements redirect people to external websites, a Microsoft-like notification claims malware infection, the message creates a reason to call immediately, and the caller requests card information and payment. This combination is more significant than any one detail alone. Even if the presenter calls it a hoax, the evidence centers on an urgent-looking infection claim and a simple route to paid assistance, which is consistent with a scam acquisition pattern.

citations.quote: Victims of the hoax are being redirected to websites through malicious advertisements.
The sites are built to display a pop-up message that looks like a Microsoft notification saying your computer is infected with malware.
The message contains a phone number that you're supposed to call to get rid of the infection.
If you call the number, you'll be speaking with crooks who ask you for your credit card.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The warning framing does not negate the red flags it places before the viewer. The opening acknowledges a fake branded notification, a phone instruction, and a card request, but simply labels them a scam. Those details still describe a highly persuasive external flow built around fear of infection and payment for a solution; the opening does not show that the flow is harmless or fictionalized.

citations.quote: The sites are built to display a pop-up message that looks like a Microsoft notification saying your computer is infected with malware.
The message contains a phone number that you're supposed to call to get rid of the infection.
To pay for their help getting rid of the malware.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These signals are evidence about the third-party hoax being exposed, not about a solicitation by the program. The segment identifies the notification as fake, identifies the callers as crooks, warns viewers not to engage, and supplies a self-help removal procedure. The presence of red flags in an investigation does not establish that the video endorses or offers the underlying transaction.

citations.quote: The problem is, it's a scam.
Don't fall for it.
That's it, you're done.

opening.argument: Although presented as technology news, the program repeatedly directs viewers into actions outside the broadcast: it tells them to go to commando.com and search for a specific story about the Facebook hack, while the broader show also asks listeners to rate the podcast so others can find it. That promotional distribution behavior, combined with a detailed description of a phone-and-credit-card remediation flow, leaves open the possibility that the security topic functions as audience steering rather than neutral reporting. The evidence supports concern about solicitation even if it does not prove every element.

citations.quote: To learn more, go to commando.com. And search for our story titled, What to Do Now Because of the Facebook Hack.
once you're done listening to our podcast,. Do us a favor and give us a good rating on wherever you're listening to us
If you call the number, you'll be speaking with crooks who ask you for your credit card.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening calls the program informational, but that does not answer why it includes explicit off-platform directions and audience-growth requests. The same presentation gives viewers a simple phone-and-payment pathway associated with malware removal. At minimum, those calls to action mean the commercial or promotional function is not excluded merely because the host uses news language.

citations.quote: To learn more, go to commando.com.
give us a good rating on wherever you're listening to us.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The external direction is to the program's own explanatory story, not to the phone number or the alleged operators. The rating request promotes the podcast, while the scam segment tells viewers not to call and explains how to close the pop-up themselves. Nothing quoted links the program's calls to action to payment, rewards, or acquisition from viewers.

citations.quote: To learn more, go to commando.com. And search for our story titled, What to Do Now Because of the Facebook Hack.
Don't fall for it.
But don't worry, it's pretty easy to remove it yourself.
